comment.body: There's an important distinction here in terms of capital return. Korea passed a new law designating certain "large dividend payers". Essentially, if highly profitable companies pledge to pay large dividends and continually increase their dividend, it gets recharacterized as a return of capital instead of a dividend, which can make it almost tax free for native Koreans. Samsung is already on track for this, and Hynix is likely laying the groundwork to gain this tax treatment next year. The reason I say this is because of Hynix's relatively light buyback number tonight, I think tonight is hinting that moving forward they will probably conduct an equal split between buybacks and dividends rather than pure buybacks.

comment.body:
Lastly, our Japanese share repurchaser, SE Holdings and Incubations (9478) just wrapped up its recent share repurchase program, buying back 224,700 shares at 521 Yen from the end of July through September. While I wish they bought a bit more (they had capacity for about 300,000), only 992,000 shares traded during the period. Essentially, they are limited by trading activity to around 25% of the volume, (they bought 22%), so really can't complain. Like clockwork, SE tends to fade into results before the new repurchase programs are announced. The time to buy, in my opinion, is before results, by the time a new repurchase program is announced, it's already too late.

The S&P is up 2% quarter-to-date, and the Topix Value Index is up 4% quarter-to-date, so I am anticipating a smaller, but stable quarter of investment performance. With an estimated Tangible Book Value of 795 Yen, I want to keep entries disciplined, so I continually buy under 530, which represents two thirds of Tangible Book Value. Given the company was repurchasing at an average price of 520, I think it tilts the odds in your favor, even if results are underwhelming in October, the repurchase will help keep the stock up and also generate further Tangible Book Value growth. SE is a name I am perpetually bullish on, I really do like Japanese equities, and the ability to buy someone who primarily owns Japanese equities at 50% upside to book, while they are repurchasing 2-3% of the float each quarter, is practically unheard of. If you ever find similar setups, please inform me

comment.body: On a side note, to anyone who held HRTG - congratulations. Great results of $2 a share, but honestly this shouldn't really come as s surprise, last quarter's "miss" was due to winter storms and Q2 was much calmer. One of the reason I have been letting positions "ride" is because the volatility this year has been immense as short-term traders and pods turn earnings into a casino. A few weeks ago $ASIC was $17.50 and discarded trash - now it's up 40% despite not much of a change. HRTG is similar - $21 to $31 in less than 6 weeks. Letting positions ride obviously has hurt in Kioxia, WDC, Samsung, and Hynix, if I used a uniform 15% stop I would've saved myself a lot. Still, I think every once in a while you need to bend the rules, and given the immense volatility I am giving my trades a bit more leeway than I normally would, and am trying to balance things out with a higher than normal cash pile. Today, it obviously sucks getting slammed while the market is relative unchanged, but I think a little perspective is warranted. Can't run 20 points ahead of the S&P without some heartache

comment.body:
I’ve been a heavy Codex and Claude Code user for the last six months, using Max/Pro subscriptions.
Both underlying model lineups are incredibly strong, and the Codex vs. Claude Code debate seems to me to be mostly a matter of taste. Both have their quirks.
But one clear distinction is that OpenAI doesn’t seem nearly as compute-constrained. The limits are much more generous, they reset more often, and users can even “save” resets for later.
I can easily get 4–5x more tokens out of my Codex subscription than from the Anthropic one.

JPM ER Discussion (FWIW)

Samsung Electronics
2Q26 headline results beat; focus on durability of earnings cycle beyond 2H26

Overweight 005930.KS, 005930 KS Price (07 Jul 26):W299,000 Price Target (Dec-26):W480,000
Samsung Electronics (SEC) disclosed 2Q26 headline results above the recently revised-down consensus estimate after recognizing W15+trn worth of labor cost provisions covering the two quarters of 1H26. Given our bullish view on the near-term memory market S-D (i.e. CPU taking over LPDDR supply with demand upward revision and ongoing enterprise SSD order strength), we continue to see memory pricing in favor of suppliers and expect another leg of upward EPS revisions. The current share price (SEC shares are trading at 5.2x FTM P/E, the cheapest memory stock globally) appears to price in only a little of the structural S&D dynamic shifts (e.g., multi-year shortage, growing LTA mix, and other factors). We reiterate our bullish “longer for higher up-cycle” view on the memory industry and SEC shares, and recommend investors accumulate. The company is likely to disclose the full earnings details on July 30, Asia morning time.
Record-breaking results and consensus beats, albeit on a labor cost provisions. SEC’s 2Q26 headline OP of W89.4trn came in above recently lowered Street estimates of W75trn-84trn and headline consensus, likely thanks to better-than-expected memory price strength and Won depreciation. On memory pricing, we believe NAND blended ASP trends (above 70% Q/Q increase vs. JPMe +53% Q/Q) have been better than our expectations vs. DRAM being below our estimate of a high-50s% Q/Q increase due mainly to the product mix. We believe the overall volume sales must have been slightly better than the initial guidance if the company used some strategic inventory (more on DRAM than NAND). On the LSI/foundry side, 4nm HBM4 base-die production appears to have entered full-scale mass production supporting the top-line trends; however, we expect the overall division earnings to have widened the loss due, mainly to one-off labor cost provisions. As for the set business, it remains unclear if the MX division has turned into a loss-making one, but we believe y-y margin deterioration is accelerating with greater pressure from component price hikes.
Diverging operational momentum continues, with memory ASP strength to lead to further EPS upgrades from 2H26 onwards. We expect the memory-led earnings structure to continue in 2H26 (i.e. greater divergence between memory and non-memory businesses) and view the memory pricing forecast to be the most important variable that dictates the earnings outlook. As memory sufficiency remains extremely low (50-60% of procurement is only met via supply), the pricing environment is likely to remain favorable in 2H26. Yet, we are witnessing an increase in customer pushback due to substantial BOM cost pressure, and expect server-driven memory consumption trends to accelerate, implying lower volume allocation to consumer electronic customers. Between DRAM and NAND, we believe NAND pricing could surprise on the upside relative to investor expectations (20% +/- q-q increase) given U.S. hyperscalers’ appetite for sourcing eSSD for KV cache offloading purposes.
Chip shortage broadening out to foundry? All eyes on Samsung Foundry’s new customer order win. Following the tightening of capacity tightness at TSMC’s leading edge foundry/packaging capacity, Samsung Foundry seems to be engaging with multiple new customers for AI chip projects; according to press release – Google, Anthropic, Meta, AMD, BYD, and others; for potential order discussions. This is on top of its order win for Tesla AI5/AI6 chips (note) and the Apple CIS (note) partnership. Such customer order wins could help Samsung’s foundry division's utilization rate move up to the full run rate with the need for additional capacity buildout at the U.S. Taylor fab, in our view. From the recent Korea AI mega-investment master plan announcement (note), there was little information about the foundry investment roadmap. After the labor cost settlement terms, we view the fixed cost pressure on the foundry/LSI division as greater vs. the past and believe new order wins are critical for a sustainable business turnaround.
Investors will focus on the durability of earnings and look forward to a long-term strategy update (incl. LTA progress). Looking at SEC’s FTM P/E trend in 1H26, it remained 3-6x (or 3.2x during 1Q26 and 4.8x during 2Q26) implying a peak-cycle multiple with high skepticism on the sustainability of earnings in the following year (i.e., SEC shares are still at an inflection point between de-rating and multiple normalization). Compared to 1H26, 2H26 price H-H momentum will likely be slower due to a higher base effect, and suppliers will initiate LTA discussions more actively with key customers (mainly CSP customers) amidst accelerating infrastructure investment. Provided there is an unprecedented shortage, we may see several different procurement initiatives from key customers (balancing the new server platform specs); however, none of these will be an alarm to the demand signal, and we view the memory side of the S-D equation as very healthy. We view investors as having underestimated the duration of the elongated up-cycle and remain constructive on SEC and memory stock fundamentals and risk-reward on a medium-term horizon on the recent pullback.
Potential next key catalysts: (1) CSP commentary on AI service business model progress and consequent hardware capex spending update; (2) AI ecosystem funding progress update (esp. CSP and AI foundation model players’ capex-related funding needs); (3) memory LTA progress update (key headlines such as percentage of coverage, volume vs. pricing guarantee, and ceiling/floor price as well as target margin); and (4) memory technology commentary update (KV cache offloading related memory tiering concept specifics update heading into agents-to-agents interaction vs. memory spending optimization initiatives from software stack level). For SEC specifically, we also note a 2024A-2026E shareholder return update (how much of the 2026E FCF is returned as a split between buyback and dividend; JPMe: over W110trn total shareholder return pool) and the following 2027-2029 shareholder return update (whether SEC connects the concept of sustainable earnings to LTA and business structure changes and if it provides a more progressive stance on the total amount and duration of return) to be critical elements to the 2H26 share price outlook.

Samsung Electronics (Overweight; Price Target: W480,000)
Investment Thesis
We are OW on SEC given the profit growth cycle is reaccelerating due to improving legacy fundamentals. Although our view on SEC’s HBM business execution remains conservative, given the lack of evidence of its regaining its technology moat (1cnm), we believe its improving HBM qualification progress tactically bodes well for its near- to mid-term share price trajectory amid a positive industry setup. In order for SEC’s shares to be fundamentally even more appealing, we believe increasing evidence of its technology leadership is required to restore investor confidence.
Valuation
Our Dec-26 PT of W480K based on a mid-cycle P/E valuation: 8x FY26E-27E P/E (vs. 6x down-cycle and 10x up-cycle).
Risks to Rating and Price Target
Downside risks to our rating and price target include: (1) an elongated memory price downcycle; (2) weaker-than-expected HBM demand from ASIC customers in FY25-26E; (3) delayed HBM qualification for future product generations; and (4) slower-than-expected mobile unit growth.

Given our bullish view on the near-term memory market S-D (i.e. CPU taking over LPDDR supply with demand upward revision and ongoing enterprise SSD order strength), we continue to see memory pricing in favor of suppliers and expect another leg of upward EPS revisions. The current share price (SEC shares are trading at 5.2x FTM P/E, the cheapest memory stock globally) appears to price in only a little of the structural S&D dynamic shifts (e.g., multi-year shortage, growing LTA mix, and other factors). We reiterate our bullish “longer for higher up-cycle” view on the memory industry and SEC shares, and recommend investors accumulate. The company is likely to disclose the full earnings details on July 30, Asia morning time.
Record-breaking results and consensus beats, albeit on a labor cost provisions. SEC’s 2Q26 headline OP of W89.4trn came in above recently lowered Street estimates of W75trn-84trn and headline consensus, likely thanks to better-than-expected memory price strength and Won depreciation. On memory pricing, we believe NAND blended ASP trends (above 70% Q/Q increase vs. JPMe +53% Q/Q) have been better than our expectations vs. DRAM being below our estimate of a high-50s% Q/Q increase due mainly to the product mix. We believe the overall volume sales must have been slightly better than the initial guidance if the company used some strategic inventory (more on DRAM than NAND). On the LSI/foundry side, 4nm HBM4 base-die production appears to have entered full-scale mass production supporting the top-line trends; however, we expect the overall division earnings to have widened the loss due, mainly to one-off labor cost provisions. As for the set business, it remains unclear if the MX division has turned into a loss-making one, but we believe y-y margin deterioration is accelerating with greater pressure from component price hikes.
Diverging operational momentum continues, with memory ASP strength to lead to further EPS upgrades from 2H26 onwards. We expect the memory-led earnings structure to continue in 2H26 (i.e. greater divergence between memory and non-memory businesses) and view the memory pricing forecast to be the most important variable that dictates the earnings outlook. As memory sufficiency remains extremely low (50-60% of procurement is only met via supply), the pricing environment is likely to remain favorable in 2H26. Yet, we are witnessing an increase in customer pushback due to substantial BOM cost pressure, and expect server-driven memory consumption trends to accelerate, implying lower volume allocation to consumer electronic customers. Between DRAM and NAND, we believe NAND pricing could surprise on the upside relative to investor expectations (20% +/- q-q increase) given U.S. hyperscalers’ appetite for sourcing eSSD for KV cache offloading purposes.
Chip shortage broadening out to foundry? All eyes on Samsung Foundry’s new customer order win. Following the tightening of capacity tightness at TSMC’s leading edge foundry/packaging capacity, Samsung Foundry seems to be engaging with multiple new customers for AI chip projects; according to press release – Google, Anthropic, Meta, AMD, BYD, and others; for potential order discussions. This is on top of its order win for Tesla AI5/AI6 chips (note) and the Apple CIS (note) partnership. Such customer order wins could help Samsung’s foundry division's utilization rate move up to the full run rate with the need for additional capacity buildout at the U.S. Taylor fab, in our view. From the recent Korea AI mega-investment master plan announcement (note), there was little information about the foundry investment roadmap. After the labor cost settlement terms, we view the fixed cost pressure on the foundry/LSI division as greater vs. the past and believe new order wins are critical for a sustainable business turnaround.
Investors will focus on the durability of earnings and look forward to a long-term strategy update (incl. LTA progress). Looking at SEC’s FTM P/E trend in 1H26, it remained 3-6x (or 3.2x during 1Q26 and 4.8x during 2Q26) implying a peak-cycle multiple with high skepticism on the sustainability of earnings in the following year (i.e., SEC shares are still at an inflection point between de-rating and multiple normalization). Compared to 1H26, 2H26 price H-H momentum will likely be slower due to a higher base effect, and suppliers will initiate LTA discussions more actively with key customers (mainly CSP customers) amidst accelerating infrastructure investment. Provided there is an unprecedented shortage, we may see several different procurement initiatives from key customers (balancing the new server platform specs); however, none of these will be an alarm to the demand signal, and we view the memory side of the S-D equation as very healthy. We view investors as having underestimated the duration of the elongated up-cycle and remain constructive on SEC and memory stock fundamentals and risk-reward on a medium-term horizon on the recent pullback.
Potential next key catalysts: (1) CSP commentary on AI service business model progress and consequent hardware capex spending update; (2) AI ecosystem funding progress update (esp. CSP and AI foundation model players’ capex-related funding needs); (3) memory LTA progress update (key headlines such as percentage of coverage, volume vs. pricing guarantee, and ceiling/floor price as well as target margin); and (4) memory technology commentary update (KV cache offloading related memory tiering concept specifics update heading into agents-to-agents interaction vs. memory spending optimization initiatives from software stack level). For SEC specifically, we also note a 2024A-2026E shareholder return update (how much of the 2026E FCF is returned as a split between buyback and dividend; JPMe: over W110trn total shareholder return pool) and the following 2027-2029 shareholder return update (whether SEC connects the concept of sustainable earnings to LTA and business structure changes and if it provides a more progressive stance on the total amount and duration of return) to be critical elements to the 2H26 share price outlook.

Samsung Electronics (Overweight; Price Target: W480,000)
Investment Thesis
We are OW on SEC given the profit growth cycle is reaccelerating due to improving legacy fundamentals. Although our view on SEC’s HBM business execution remains conservative, given the lack of evidence of its regaining its technology moat (1cnm), we believe its improving HBM qualification progress tactically bodes well for its near- to mid-term share price trajectory amid a positive industry setup. In order for SEC’s shares to be fundamentally even more appealing, we believe increasing evidence of its technology leadership is required to restore investor confidence.
Valuation
Our Dec-26 PT of W480K based on a mid-cycle P/E valuation: 8x FY26E-27E P/E (vs. 6x down-cycle and 10x up-cycle).
Risks to Rating and Price Target
Downside risks to our rating and price target include: (1) an elongated memory price downcycle; (2) weaker-than-expected HBM demand from ASIC customers in FY25-26E; (3) delayed HBM qualification for future product generations; and (4) slower-than-expected mobile unit growth.

comment.body:
I think the HDD point is directionally right but overstated.

HDD is not the AI bottleneck. It is the cheap-capacity layer that benefits from AI data exhaust. Useful, yes. But the marginal constraint in AI is overwhelmingly memory bandwidth, memory capacity, latency, compute locality, and power efficiency. That points to HBM/DRAM/LPDDR/GDDR/NAND far more directly than HDD.

Physical AI makes this even more obvious. Robots, drones, autonomous vehicles, factories, and multimodal edge systems are real-time inference/control systems. They are not waiting on spinning disks. They need fast memory, local NAND buffering, accelerators, and networking. HDD only shows up later in the backend as cold/warm storage for fleet logs, video archives, backups, and retained training data.

So WDC can be a good trade without being a better AI demand play than memory. Anyways, I’m long both now (joined on WDC after the dip lol).

They can afford to fumble around and still be in pole position to own the orchestration/harness layer. Altho the "killer AI device" is still being worked on I think our phones will prove to be the true AI device. 

Apple's prowess in silicon is also incredibly impresive so i think they have a huge edge for on device compute. Over a medium horizon 3-5 years the ability to run locally hosted models for simpler / agentic tasks will be critical and Apple will be a big leader here. 

So I agree its expensive but I think the moat is rock solid and the proliferation of quality open source models is actually helping them big time. 

Owning the hardware makes you the prime candidate to extract an orchestration tax (think 30% app store tax for the AI era)

Three other thoughts on price action
- MOMO likely to be a little weak today and tomorrow because the share repurchases are usually paused on earnings days
- CRWV interesting to see if it can break through 130 and follow NBIS higher. CRWV insiders tend to unload at 120, I expect we will see a Form 4 from Magnetar indicating they dumped another million a day above 120, that is where they usually sell
- IESC Billionaire owner Gendell might continue trimming above 700, but I am not concerned. It's more than 60% of his fund, Tontine Asset Manangement, and so I think it is just a bit of risk management and balancing he is doing. I really don't mind when guys who have built something from nothing and are worth billions sell 1 or 2% of their position. It's natural to cash in a bit. Summary: Samsung's structural advantages over SK Hynix and Micron in HBM come down to vertical integration — they're the only player that controls everything from DRAM fab to logic foundry to silicon photonics under one roof. Here's how each advantage breaks down:
1. In-House Logic Foundry for the Base Die
This is the biggest one. HBM4 requires a logic base die (the "brain" of the stack) built on an advanced foundry process — not a DRAM process. SK Hynix had to go to TSMC (and controversially picked N12, a relatively old node), while Micron attempted to use its internal DRAM process — both decisions hurt them in HBM4 qualification.
Samsung can manufacture its own HBM4 logic die using its SF4X 4nm process in-house. This gives Samsung:
Faster iteration cycles — no dependency on TSMC's capacity or scheduling
Lower cost — no TSMC margin embedded in the base die
Custom IP co-design — hyperscalers like Meta and Microsoft can embed their own IP directly into Samsung's HBM4 base die, which is increasingly what Big Tech wants
Samsung is reportedly already moving next-gen custom HBM logic dies to its 2nm process node — SK Hynix's TSMC N12 is four generations behind that
The SF4X 4nm base die yield has already exceeded 40% in test production, which engineers consider a strong starting point for mass production ramp.
2. Logic Design Experience
Because Samsung has been running a foundry and designing logic chips (NVMe controllers, Exynos SoCs, etc.), they have signal integrity and high-speed interface IP expertise that SK Hynix and Micron simply don't have. The HBM4 PHY — the interface between the base die and the GPU — is fundamentally a logic design problem, not a DRAM design problem. Samsung's engineers have been doing this for years; SK Hynix and Micron are learning it from scratch.
3. Internal Silicon Photonics (SiPho) + CPO Capability
Samsung Foundry has an internal silicon photonics process node and a dedicated CPO (co-packaged optics) design group. This is the long-term moat. As the article argues — and as Nvidia's ISSCC 2026 demo confirmed — the future of memory disaggregation runs through optical interconnects. Samsung is the only DRAM vendor with in-house SiPho capability, positioning them to co-design HBM PHY, TSV layout, and optical engines simultaneously.
4. Next-Gen DRAM Node (1c)
For the DRAM die stacks themselves, Samsung is targeting 1c-generation DRAM (10nm-class 6th gen) for HBM4, while SK Hynix is currently using 1b DRAM. If Samsung stabilizes 1c DRAM in volume, the resulting HBM4 products would have a density and power advantage over SK Hynix's current stacks.
The Honest Caveat
Samsung is playing catch-up on execution. SK Hynix still holds ~70% HBM market share because they've been winning Nvidia qualifications consistently since HBM2e. Samsung stumbled badly on HBM3e — the article notes this explicitly, and it's why SK Hynix briefly took the #1 overall DRAM market share position from Samsung for the first time ever. The structural advantages above are forward-looking bets on HBM4 and beyond, not current market position.
The core thesis from the article is essentially: Samsung lost the HBM3e battle but is better-equipped to win the HBM4 war — because HBM4 is fundamentally a logic engineering problem, and that's Samsung's home turf.

comment.body: They reinsured at a lower cost because reinsurance rates for FL have plummeted. Overall losses in FL are down huge (insurers are making a lot of cash) so the reinsurers want in on the action and are dropping rates 15-20%. This is a tailwind for the primary insurers, rates might be declining 5-10%, but reinsurance costs are falling at double the rate. HRTG will take some time, I really don't anticipate it trading below year end book value (which should be 20-21). Conditions in their geographies are great, they are growing, and they should have a bunch of excess capital to return. The stock kind of has a mind of its own, I've been in and out since 6 a share in 2023 and it frequently has spasms where it makes moves that don't make too much sense. It's 3% of my portfolio right now, frustrating to see it (along with Itafos and OSB) lag, but I am not giving up on it, or those other two

comment.body:
@Cluseau Research I saw your post re: Coreweave. It is a new position for me so thought I would have some fun laying out a quick thesis on why I started a mid sized position

The core issue with Neos is the extreme capital investment, dilution needed to get there and how to deal with depreciation of chips

The solution to all of these is scale and quality - this is where Coreweave shines

Coreweave - The Biggest Neo on the Block
- ~55B MC + 25B debt
- 1.5 GW online scaling to 3.5 GW by '28 (most already permitted)

- Novel capital structure with asset level recourse and rates now 7.5% from 15% originally
- Very strong NVDA connection (equity investment, backstopping compute and top generation chip access)
- Amazing blue chip client list (MSFT, OpenAI, Jane St, Meta & now Anthropic) with $100B backlog
- Market says Coreweave product is top tier and commands a strong premium from customers which will matter more when contracts come up for renewal and compute is less scarce 

Numbers:
- Rev: $12B '26 --> $25B in 27 and 30-35B in '28
- 50-60% EBITDA margins = ~$18B EBITDA in '28
- $18B EBITDA minus $3B interest minus $9B D&A = ~$6B Op Income or ~$9/share (or 15-20% net margin)
- ~60B of capex needed; $40B from OCF (huge advantage) / $15B via debt / $5B via equity estimated
- Assume FD shares 550 --> 650 by '28 and debt $25B --> $40B; MC = $65B + $40B Debt = $105B EV
- On '28 Numbers Coreweave is: ~6x EV/EBITDA; 3x Rev/EV and ~11.5x PE
- I think 50-100% upside from here is very reasonable and the dilution/execution risk is much much lower than almost every other neo 

In short you are getting the market leader at a discount due to margins compressing from the capacity ramp. This ramp is what every other neo needs to do in order to hit their growth projections. Scale/Quality/Cash Flow help the durability of the business and dilution has mostly occured already so OCF will help fund the majority of the build out.

As a last point - I look to hyperscalers cloud segment for a guideline on what end state metrics could look like for cloud providers. GCP at ~$80B rev did 60% YoY rev growth which led to 3x op income growth. My take away is that very very large scale is the key to neo's. Even at $35B Coreweave will be just entering the realm of real profitability - at $40-50B new revenue is VERY accretive so focusing on scale is key.

Before anyone asks NBIS is also top tier but has the same valuation and is still earlier in the ramp than Coreweave

comment.body:
@Cluseau Research wondering if you ever had a chance to revisit PSIX? 

I know it has some painful memories but given how red hot power is and the first ever conference call I think we may be about to re-rate

My elevator pitch for fresh eyes:

$PSIX
- Creates enclosures for AWS data centres using gensets from GNRC and CAT (engine agnostic)
- Diesel fired for back up power now transitioning to nat gas for prime power = higher complexity, higher margin
- Was a darling last year due to amazing growth but cratered after Q3/4 slowdown and margin compression
- Margins have troughed ~21% with target for 25% and rev still growing 20-30% in '26
- Trades at 15x '26 EPS and maybe ~10x '28 EPS (true GARP name)
- First EVER conference call on Monday which is hopefully the catalyst to re-rate this like other power names
- Only 1.6B market cap trading at ~2x trailing rev

comment.body: I'm not interested in ACIC. ACIC is notably different from HRTG, they almost exclusively provide insurance to large apartment buildings. That market is extremely competitive, and reprices very quickly. For example, a homeowner with a $3,000 policy doesn't really care if a comparable quote is $2,900, because the cost of inspection and paperwork isn't really worth it to them. For a big apartment complex where rates might drop from $600,000 to $540,000, they are almost certainly going to take that deal. And so I think ACIC is likely to have a tougher next few years compared to peers who focus on smaller homes

Company has been returning excess profits via special dividends, paid a 21 cent distribution recently

comment.body:
Some are claiming that's the case. See here: https://x.com/RihardJarc/status/2037134084833464492

"The paper has benchmarked the 8x performance increase in computing attention when there is an FP32 setup and a 6x memory reduction assessment on the FP16 baseline. Frontier AI labs do not run FP32/FP16 KV cache for inference in production today. Most of the inference on leading AI labs is run on FP8, some even FP4, so the claimed savings on HBM are much lower if you compare them to actual current productions. Also, every frontier AI lab is already compressing their KV cache as much as they can before this paper was published (this is nothing new in terms of the direction of the market). So the savings compared to what is being used mostly today are smaller than the 8x and 6x numbers."

I think the very fact that the paper was out a year ago tells you all you need to know. These labs are hiring the world's most motivated supergeniuses to build for a market they believe is worth endless billions. I find it inconceivable that they overlooked it until Google did a press release.

comment.body:
YEXT (YEXT) is conducting a sizeable tender: $140 million of stock between $5.75 and $6.50, with preference for odd-lot holders (99 shares or fewer). The tender concludes on Wednesday, March 18, 2026, which means that if you purchase 99 shares today, you should be able to tender them via IBKR once they settle tomorrow.

In my past experience, the only broker you can really trust for these types of situations is IBKR. Fidelity, Schwab, and others all require phone calls, and they occasionally get tenders wrong. You don't want to get stuck holding shares if they don't process the transaction correctly.

I purchased 99 shares of Yext on Friday, and today the corporate action was already available in the Corporate Action Manager. On IBKR, you can find the Corporate Action Manager by going to:

> Get Help (Top Right Corner)
> Scroll Down, Corporate Action Manager
> Choice Actions
> YEXT INC Tender

Once the window opens, look for row 2, “Submit shares for tender at No Specified Price,” and enter 99 shares (or fewer if you've purchased fewer).

There is a small chance Yext cancels the tender, or perhaps removes the odd-lot provision, which would mean that only a prorated portion of your 99 shares would be accepted at $5.75. Still, I think the odds of this are low, and with just two days to go until the tender closes and the stock currently trading at $5.45, a $30 profit has me interested. You are essentially risking $540 today ($5.45 × 99 shares) to get $570 back early next week, if everything goes according to plan.

I wouldn't really be interested above $5.55 or $5.65, but a $30 profit at current levels seems attractive relative to the small probability that the offer is canceled and the stock drops below $5. Once again, IBKR is the only broker I'd feel comfortable using for this trade, since the corporate action should be available online by tomorrow if you purchase today. For other brokers, I am not sure the phone call and the risk of incorrect processing are worth it.

comment.body:
There has been a significant shift in the Google and PayPal partnership recently, centered on two major announcements that fundamentally change how PayPal handles Google transactions.
1. Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) Integration (January 2026)
In early January 2026, PayPal announced it would support Google’s new Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP). This is a massive update for "agentic commerce"—shopping driven by AI.
 * AI-Powered Checkout: You will soon be able to use PayPal as a payment option directly within Google Search and the Gemini app.
 * Direct Purchases: Instead of clicking through to a merchant's website, you can complete a purchase using PayPal right while researching a product in "AI Mode."
 * Interoperability: This protocol allows merchants to list products that are "instantly purchasable" across Google’s ecosystem without needing separate integrations for every platform.
2. Multiyear Strategic Partnership (September 2025)
This followed a broader deal from late 2025 where Google named PayPal a primary payment processor.
 * Backend Processing: PayPal Enterprise Payments is now a key provider for processing card payments across Google Cloud, Google Ads, and Google Play.
 * Deeper Embedding: PayPal’s branded checkout, Hyperwallet, and Payouts are being integrated more deeply into Google's core products to make transactions more seamless.
 * Cloud Migration: As part of the deal, PayPal is migrating much of its own infrastructure to Google Cloud to help process thousands of transactions per second, especially during high-traffic events like Black Friday.
Why this matters
This move is largely about "Agentic Commerce." Both companies are betting that the future of shopping isn't just searching for links, but having an AI agent find, compare, and actually buy the item for you. By integrating at the protocol level, PayPal remains the "trust layer" for those automated transactions.
Would you like me to look into how this affects merchant fees or how to set it up for a business?

I'll be adding as this overblown narrative plays out.

comment.body:
What it proves is that for 20k and 2 months of time it was possible to build a compiler that actually compiles the Linux kernel. I know no one who could have done that unassisted in 2 months before. I know very very few ppl that could have done it at all given unlimited time. Now I can do it myself, because I learned enough about compiler theory at university and have enough practical experience that I can prompt the LLM into doing the actual hard work for me. "This changes everything". I don't care about random people off  the street, I care about the distribution of "skill" in the population of available software devs. A ton of ppl that were basically "useless warm bodies" that shipped one JIRA ticket a week are now either (soon to be) unemployed, or they level up with AI and increase their speed. A ton of ppl that were "senior staff engineer architect gatekeeper" now become less relevant since I can actually change architecture of a system in reasonable timeframes. The cost of decisions has gone down, in Bezos decision making framework the set of reversible ("two-way door") decisions has increased while the set of irreversible ("one-way door") has decreased. That means competitive moats of existing companies/software that was built on it being a large existing system (buy vs build) with lots of experience has gone down (not to zero obviously).

I do still hold Bravura Solutions ($BVS.AX) because I do think their moat is in the whole regulatory/compliance edge. But I do think Atlassian ($TEAM) vs Linear has changed - because these tools already are quite extremely buggy, so what's the worst that happens if they get a bit more buggy but move faster? Nothing. So there's gonna be much more innovation there, I would not want to bet on Atlassian winning.

And what it means for individual devs, I do think the cosy time of earning a lot and working little because of domain experience and generally being in demand is changing - IMHO the 10xers now become idk 20x/100x-ers,while the 1x-ers become 0x-ers since their job is eaten up "from the bottom".

comment.body: This might be a good short-term trade, but I'm going to be the contra and say that's just the market being reactionary. Every SaaS company can add AI features, and the existing players benefit from existing customer base, domain knowledge, brand... It can't make sense for companies like Anthropic and OpenAI to tackle dozens of different use-cases. I'm sure there will be some SaaS losers, e.g. due to poor execution, AI fundamentally changing the business, or somebody else having essential datasets. But I think in most cases, AI is great for existing SaaS businesses. Allows them to provide lots of additional value, which they can charge for. The big-picture is more money to SaaS providers; less to payroll.

comment.body:
Hehe we discussed Adobe on Twitter some time back, and I now tend to think you were right and I was wrong  :)  But I think the situation is polarised, and both perspectives can be right.

For one-shot stuff, like "make me an image" or "draft me a contract", I agree with you. I don't see anybody having a great moat. It's a crap business – a race to the bottom.

For a company like Clio, providing operational software for legal practices, is the opposite. Their software is complex, you can't just copy it, and it's a big PITA for customers to switch. And with AI, Clio will be able to provide a huge amount of additional value in the coming years, and charge for it. All they have to do is execute and the business should explode. I think this will be the norm for deeply embedded B2B SaaS.

And with AI, Clio will be able to provide a huge amount of additional value in the coming years, and charge for it. All they have to do is execute and the business should explode. I think this will be the norm for deeply embedded B2B SaaS.

comment.body: Great quarter out of CBNA. Earnings $0.81 vs $0.75. Deposit growth was wild, $210 Million in the quarter, plus another $210 Million in One-Way Sell Deposits. As a reminder, CBNA is a bank for GOP Aligned Political Organizations, and they park this case in T-Bills and Reserves to earn free money. Sometimes, they get so much deposits that they can't keep it all, and route it to other banks (One-Way Sell Deposits) using the Intrafi system. Normally, deposit growth flounders until midterms, but deposit growth is skyrocketing due to aggressive fundraising techniques. Interestingly, Trump's PACs also bank with JP Morgan Chase, given Trump announced he is suing them last week, chances are they shift more inflows to Chain Bridge. With deposits skyrocketing this far away from the midterms, Chain Bridge represents a way to play the house. They simply collect free income off of political viciousness, and given the stunning deposits report this quarter, and the prospect of fewer rate cuts I expect analyst estimates to increase. CBNA trades at just a slight premium to Tangible Book Value of around $26 a share, and given these excellent results I think it should trade around 1.4x, which implies $36 a share.

Okay, the Bolivar mine flood is reducing production materially.  Approx 300k oz per quarter.  So, 25% increase in production for silver.  Usually runs 1.6m oz a quarter.  These companies all use AgEq but the recent run in silver prices has heavily distorted these numbers and they should not be relied up. So 
1.6m oz of silver  + 21,500 tons of zinc + 2,600t of lead and 300 tons of copper = $200m per quarter.  So if silver holds, I think $100m of fcf per quarter.

comment.body: I wouldn't say I focus 100% on banks and insurance, they make up about half my portfolio and I still like to have a decent chunk of ETFs and a smaller sliver of tech and global names. It's overall a rough sector, but what I really like is the plethora of data you can use to inform your decisions. Unlike tech or consumer where brands or companies have significant individual factors, banks report such a large quantity of data on credit quality, interest rate sensitivity, deposit growth, that you can make decent apples to apples comparisons and separate the outperformers from the average names and the losers. It's also a really rational sector, so you can go long your favorites and short the benchmark or losers and not worry too much about squeeze risk. Off the top of my head, there are maybe a handful of meme banks or insurers, but the sector is largely rational so you can get an edge by purchasing the fundamental outperformers and giving them some time, and if you want to hedge them out, putting on an overall banking or insurance hedge

comment.body: 1. Kaspi KSPI - I have traded Kaspi on and off with little success. Their recent earnings were very strong and they announced a $100 Million buyback along with a hint the dividend may be reinstated early next year. I think the move from $100 to $75 was driven by concern over capital allocation, the company hinted this year it was focused on growth and its HEPS (Turkey) acquisition and the stock tanked as the dividend was eliminated and repurchases were shut down. With $100 Million in buyback activity, and the potential resumption of the dividend, I think KSPI is too cheap at 7x earnings to ignore. If it resumes the dividend at $1.50 (lower than the previous $1.60 - $1.90 range), it represents a yield of 8%, not bad for a name growing earnings at 10% a year. The Kaspi founder is heavily involved and owns almost 50%, I think the company is an outperformer with an innovative product (grocery, taxi, banking, and payments) all in one app, and that the resumption of the buyback may mark a bottom in the stock. I also find the KZT currency attractive, while inflation is high, Kazakhstan is a net exporter and higher gold and uranium prices may help it claw back some currency weakness. I added it at 0.5% weight today and leaving more room to add at $70. I put my stop at $65, and am looking for upside to $80.

comment.body: 4. Legato Acqusition LEGT - Noticed a lot of unusual volume in the stock, and the associated warrants. The trust value of the SPAC is $10.77, and likely to increase to $10.85 at the end of the quarter, so downside at $11.15 is really limited to about 3% or 30 cents. You can never predict these things 100% (just like THS, could go either way), but the elevated volume in the warrants and stock leads me to believe a deal is in the works, and rumors are swirling. Similar to BACQ (which we made 15% on), the setup very positively skewed. Good deal announced, maybe spikes to $12 or higher and provides an immediate opportunity to close at a profit if you are not a believer in the deal. Bad deal or no deal, downside is just 3% and you can redeem. This could be a fake out driven by a large investor moving the warrants, but with just 3% downside I think an attractive setup is present. Given the stock may do nothing for the next couple of months if no deal is announced, you want to be conservative on a potential entry. I wouldn't pay a penny more than $11.20, which represents 35 cents above the cash value. Added at 0.5%

comment.body:
9478 – Price has cooled from 430 to 400 and I am glad it did. Company bought back 48,000 on the 29th at401, 19,200 on the 30th at 400, and 48,000 on the 31st at412. The average repurchase price was 406 Yen, and they still have capacity to buy back another 103 Million Yen of shares (approximately 250,000) at current prices.
As a long term holder, I want them to get the shares as cheap as they can. I think a few Japanese retail investors noticed the buyback and tried to front run it. With Net Asset Value of 630 and this large buyback,I think adding right where the company is (400 Yen) is a decent entry, but you want to be very slow and careful to ensure the company gets as many shares as possible. After the buyback concludes, there will be approximately 15.5 Million shares outstanding, a 10% decrease from 17.1 Million at the start of the year.

comment.body:
CBL – I am waiting to see the 13F filings that have a deadline of November 15. One of CBL’s largest holders, Taconic Capital, is shutting down its equity arm, and I suspect they were a decent chunk of late September and early October selling. Curious to see how many shares they had left at the end of September.
I am also monitoring CBL’s term loan. The bears commonly say CBL insolvent (which is why it trades at a paltry 4x FFO), but for the first time in history CBL’s term loan is actually trading above par (100). Obviously, either the bond guys are asleep at the wheel and totally clueless, or they know what they are doing and the equity is fine.
After the market close, CBL announced it has repurchased 250,000 shares around $29.50, and has topped off the repurchase program back to $25 Million, a very positive sign. With a 6% dividend yield, a fresh repurchase program, and lower interest rates providing an immediate boost to cash flow, I am looking for upside to $3, earnings should be out sometime next week.

comment.body:
The pivot from CCCX to Argentina banks was a little crazy, but paid off nicely. BBAR (my favorite) and GGAL continue to roar (I think they are close to a near term top), and I think a similar setup is building in Chilean banks.

It seems likely the next Chilean leader is either pro-market (Kast) or Libertarian (Kaiser). The names I have purchased are Banco de Chile (BCH) and Banco Santander Chile (BSAC). They’re both trading around 12x, much more reasonable than Argentinian banks, and I think interest will build as we inch closer to mid-November (election is November 16). If you are looking for a more broad based setup, MSCI Chile ETF (ECH) is around 14x forward earnings.

Pretty funny, discussed here last week how their 10% stake in St Georges Mining (SGQ Australia) was overlooked. Almost immediately after, press release came out saying they liquidated almost the entirety of their position for $18 Million USD, and exercised their options to buy 80 Million shares at 4 cents (which they will probably sell for additional net cash proceeds of $4 Million USD)

comment.body:
3. Se Holdings (9478)

Se Holdings downgraded their earnings forecasts last night, so the name is likely to open weak later tonight.

I don't care about their publishing business.  80% of the value creation / profit comes from their equities portfolio, but a lot of Japanese investors don't realize this and pay attention to the non-adjusted numbers. SE Holdings has 560 Yen of equity securities per share (greater than the market cap), and they fund a small chunk of this via margin loans in USD, EUR, and HKD. The Japanese yen declined from 143 to 147 in Q3, so they will book a "FX Loss" since the value of their margin loans becomes larger in JPY. In their guidance update, they specifically mention this via "The Impact of Exchange Rates".

I think of SE as a closed end fund, with a small publishing business attached. Whether the publishing business makes 3 Yen or 4 Yen a quarter doesn't matter to me, because they make way more from rising stock markets. Last quarter, Net Assets 
per share jumped 24 Yen from 547 to 571, and given Global Stock Indicies were up around 5% in Q3 (Topix Small Cap was up 12%), I think Q3 Net Assets could come out as high as 590 - 595 a share.

365 Yen represents just 0.61x Tangible Book Value, which I think is an extremely attractive setup for a name at 5x adjusted earnings and where financing via Yen margin is just 1% a year. It requires patience, but you really can't find a name repurchasing 15% of the float each year at a better price. I have some orders in the 350 to 370 range to add on any weakness after the open.

If history is any indication, the company will announce a fresh repurchase program after reporting results this week

comment.body:
Sizing at 0.5% is generally because the investment is expected to have above-average volatility (and therefore the potential for above-average returns). If your entire portfolio consisted of 200 0.5% names, it would likely be much more volatile than the broader market -- which perhaps you want. 

However, I think many folks run a healthy mix of "safer" names at larger allocations (but perhaps lower volatility) of 2-10% (or 50% in the case of $IGIC) to balance out the portfolio.
